blocks.text: There is, however, an island opposite Syrian Tripoli which received its name from the rabbits that are common there (Canincheninsel); see Maundrell's Travels, p. 31. Yet Oedmann (Vermischte Sammlungen, fascicle 4, ch. 5, p. 49) thinks that they are not indigenous there, but were brought there from elsewhere. Russell (Natur. History of Aleppo, p. 55) attests that a few rabbits are kept at Aleppo by the Europeans living there for the use of the table. From this, however, it is not established with certainty whether these animals are indigenous in that region.
This reason for the name seems to have escaped a certain learned man in the Notes on Bruce's Travels edited by Hassencamp, p. 159, 60.

In this Stumpf has undoubtedly erred. For everyone knows that the marmot is an animal altogether peculiar to the Savoyard, Swiss, and Pyrenean Alps. Nor has anyone of those who have visited the regions of the East found that animal there. Rather, the animals in Egypt that Stumpf thinks are like Alpine mice seem to be Syrian hyraces or sorices, the ἔχινοι χερσαῖοι [echinoi chersaioi] of Aelian (book 3, ch. 10, where their foresight and skill in storing up food are recounted; cf. Bochart below, p. 1008. 3. and p. 1016), in which we find all the things that the Arabs recount of the وبر [wabr]. The size of the animal is that of a marmot, though its body is more elongated, its back marked with bristles protruding along the ridge (whence the name ἐχῖνος [echinos] was undoubtedly given to it by the Greeks), dark above, whitish below; an oblong snout; very short claws, no tail; a creeping gait, a vegetable diet; it lives in the hollows of rocks. See Schreber's Mammalia 4, plate 211 B. Under the name of the lamb of Israel (see Bochart above) Shaw described this animal (Travels, p. 301, German trans., where however Daman Israel is falsely written for Ganam Israel غنم اسرايل [ghanam isrāʾīl], an error which has crept into several other books), who found this animal frequently on Mount Lebanon and in other places of Syria. The same was known to Prospero Alpini, who mentioned a certain low-statured animal, not unlike a rabbit, which they call the lamb of Israel, in Hist. Nat. Aegypti, vol. 1, ch. 20, p. 80, and book 4, ch. 9. That the Hebrew name of this Syrian hyrax was שפן was first maintained by Shaw, loc. cit. He has recently found someone who agrees with him in Bruce, Travels, vol. 5, p. 149, Leipzig trans., who diligently describes this animal—frequently seen by him not only in Syria, but also in Ethiopia—under the name Aschkoko, by which it is called among the Amharas from the bristles protruding along the ridge of its back in the likeness of thorns (for the Amharic Aschok signifies a thorn; see Ludolf's Lexic. Amhar., p. 58). He also gave an illustration of it on plate 29. And it must be admitted that there occur in the Syrian hyrax, وبر [wabr], all the things that we read of the שפן in the Hebrew codex. For first, neither is cloven-hoofed. 2. Both ruminate; which Bruce, loc. cit., p. 148, attests was observed in an Aschkoko, that is, a hyrax, kept by him at home; cf. Levit. XI, 5. and Deut. XIV, 7. 3. Both are edible, although unclean: those of the Arabs who inhabit Lebanon and Arabia Petraea feed on the flesh of the Syrian hyrax (see the words of Mawardi, adduced by Bochart above), although the rest of the Muslims and the Christian Abyssinians abstain from it as from an unclean food. See Bruce, p. 151. 4. Both are gregarious, Bruce, p. 146; cf. Prov. XXX, 26. 5. Both are feeble, Prov., loc. cit. 6. Both have their home in the rock, Shaw, p. 301, Bruce, p. 146; cf. Ps. CIV, 18. 7. Both are common in Syria and Eretz Yisrael, on the testimony of those same travelers. Yet each of these particulars we shall also find in the jerboa (Mus iaculus), the يربوع [yarbūʿ] of the Arabs, concerning which Bochart has much in what follows.

Bruce, vol. 5, p. 144, Leipzig trans., has described this animal much more accurately than the Arabs. It is evident that it is a species of viverra, which Blumenbach in a note on that passage of Bruce calls viverra aurita, on account of its remarkable oval ears. The name of the animal was unknown to Buffon, who gave a description of it in the Supplemm. to vol. 3 of the Hist. Nat.

Yet if the وبر [wabr] is the Syrian hyrax (and we think it has been sufficiently proved that it is, above in note 3), nothing will prevent the وبر [wabr] of the Arabs and the שפן of the Hebrews from being the same animal.

Mus jaculus with an elongated tufted tail, sub-pentadactyl forefeet, very long hind legs, very short forelegs, Linnaeus, Systema Naturae, vol. 1, p. 157, 13th ed. A description of the animal, diligently observed by themselves, has been given by Hasselquist in Itinerar. Palaestinae, p. 277, Pallas in Novae Species Quadrupedum ex Glirium ordine, p. 277 ff., and Bruce in Travels, vol. 5, p. 128 ff. With whom should be compared Oedmann in the Vermischte Sammlungen, fascicle 4, p. 48.
